chest_pain.label: Chest pain

red_flags.text: Chest pain at rest or ongoing (possible heart attack - ER by ambulance, don't wait for office tests)
red_flags.source_note: Partly supported (ACC Ten Points summary only): guideline says patients with acute chest pain should call 9-1-1; it does not define Lantern's emergent tier.

red_flags.text: Chest pain with sweating, fainting or breathlessness
red_flags.source_note: Partly supported (ACC Ten Points summary only): accompanying symptoms (nausea, palpitations, breathlessness) are named; no specific sweating/fainting tier rule found.

red_flags.text: Recent chest pain with new ischemic ECG changes
red_flags.source_note: No source found for the tier (ECG and troponin are key to assess ACS, Ten Points 4-5); whether ST change is emergent when pain has resolved needs a clinician.

red_flags.text: Sudden tearing pain to the back, or sudden breathlessness / coughing blood (aortic dissection or blood clot in lung)
red_flags.source_note: Partly supported (ACC Ten Points summary only): aortic syndrome and pulmonary embolism are named as causes to consider; no tier guidance.

urgent_flags.text: New or worsening chest pain with exertion
urgent_flags.source_note: Guideline defines new or changed chest pain as 'acute chest pain' (Ten Points 1), so the 2-week tier is not guideline-backed; the pattern also does not require exertion.

decision_facts.group: Known coronary disease: prior heart attack, stent or bypass
decision_facts.why: Known coronary disease changes the testing pathway and raises concern for a new blockage

decision_facts.group: Heart risk factors: age, sex, high BP, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, family history
decision_facts.why: Guideline sorts patients into low / intermediate / high risk to decide whether testing is needed at all
Coronary CT and some tests use contrast dye, which can harm weak kidneys
Used for risk scoring and to see whether prevention is on track

decision_facts.group: Accompanying symptoms, especially in women: nausea, fatigue, breathlessness, jaw/arm/back pain
decision_facts.why: Guideline drops 'atypical'; women more often have these, and they should not lower concern

decision_facts.group: Previous ECG, stress test, coronary CT or angiogram
decision_facts.why: Recent normal testing may change what is needed; abnormal testing raises concern
decision_facts.source_note: Partly supported (ACC Ten Points summary only): recommendations branch on known CAD; 'recent normal testing may change what is needed' not found.

decision_facts.why: Shows whether prevention is on track before the visit

routing_rules.note: eGFR under 30 - contrast for coronary CT or angiography carries uncertain kidney risk; cardiology chooses the test
routing_rules.source_note: ACC 2025 'Contrast Media in Advanced Cardiovascular Imaging' calls eGFR <30 a relative contraindication; 2021 chest pain guideline wording not yet checked

not_seen: Pain clearly reproduced by pressing on the chest wall (musculoskeletal)
Reflux-type symptoms with low cardiac risk (GI)
Low-risk patient - guideline says further testing may not be needed (eConsult may be enough)
review_notes: Guideline uses 'cardiac / possible cardiac / noncardiac', not 'typical/atypical' - verify wording
Whether cp_ecg_ischemia should be emergent or urgent when pain is not current

palpitations_afib.label: Palpitations / suspected atrial fibrillation

red_flags.text: Very fast heart rate with low blood pressure or near-fainting (unstable)
Stroke symptoms (face droop, arm weakness, speech trouble)

urgent_flags.text: New AFib with a fast rate
urgent_flags.source_note: Rate cutoff >110 at rest is a draft number for clinician review (not taken from a checked guideline section).

urgent_flags.text: Palpitations with new swelling or breathlessness

decision_facts.group: Stroke-risk factors (CHA2DS2-VASc parts): heart failure, high BP, age 65-74 / 75+, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA/clot, vascular disease (prior heart attack, PAD), female sex
decision_facts.why: Drives the blood-thinner decision. Guideline recommends a blood thinner when yearly stroke risk is about 2%+ (roughly score 2+ in men, 3+ in women) - verify. Lantern shows the parts; the specialist decides.
decision_facts.source_note: Why-text uses outdated 2019 score cutoffs; the 2023 guideline frames anticoagulation around estimated annual stroke risk of about 2% or more. ESC 2024 uses CHA2DS2-VA (sex removed). Fix pending.

decision_facts.group: Bleeding-risk factors: prior bleeding, heavy alcohol, NSAID or antiplatelet use, kidney or liver disease, anemia
decision_facts.why: Weighed against stroke risk; modifiable ones should be fixed rather than used as a reason to withhold a blood thinner

decision_facts.group: Already on a blood thinner? (warfarin INR if so)
decision_facts.why: Changes the decision from 'whether' to 'is it working'
decision_facts.source_note: Partly supported (ACC Ten Points summary only): DOACs preferred over warfarin except mitral stenosis or mechanical valve; INR only matters for warfarin.

decision_facts.why: Overactive thyroid causes AFib and should be treated first
Needed to choose and dose blood thinners

decision_facts.group: AFib drivers: obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol, high BP
decision_facts.why: 2023 guideline makes risk-factor treatment a core part of AFib care

decision_facts.group: Current heart-rate medicines (beta blocker, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin)
decision_facts.why: Shows whether rate control has been tried

decision_facts.group: Known AFib and rate-control considerations: heart rate, BP, lung disease
decision_facts.why: Tells a new diagnosis from known AFib; low BP or lung disease limits which rate medicines are safe (clinician to confirm: beta-blocker caution is mainly about asthma)

routing_rules.note: TSH out of range - thyroid may explain the palpitations; consider treating thyroid / endocrinology first
routing_rules.source_note: Range: ATA 2018 (lab-dependent, ~0.4-4.5). 'Thyroid first' routing has no guideline source yet.

not_seen: Palpitations from an overactive thyroid - may go to endocrinology first
Occasional skipped beats with a normal ECG and no heart disease - often eConsult
review_notes: Exact CHA2DS2-VASc thresholds in the 2023 guideline - verify
Whether Lantern should compute the score or only list the parts

heart_failure_symptoms.label: Heart failure symptoms

red_flags.text: Breathless at rest or can't lie flat

urgent_flags.text: NT-proBNP over 2,000 ng/L (NICE: specialist + echo within 2 weeks)
Fast weight gain or worsening swelling

soon_flags.text: NT-proBNP 400-2,000 ng/L (NICE: specialist + echo within 6 weeks)

decision_facts.why: NICE uses it to set urgency: over 2,000 ng/L, specialist + echo within 2 weeks; 400-2,000, within 6 weeks. Under 400 in an untreated person makes heart failure less likely - review other causes, and discuss with a heart failure specialist if still concerned

decision_facts.group: Things that push NT-proBNP up: lung disease (incl. COPD), kidney disease, liver disease or cirrhosis, diabetes, sepsis
decision_facts.why: A high value may partly reflect these rather than heart failure (NICE lists pulmonary, renal, liver and systemic causes)
decision_facts.source_note: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF Table 6 also lists advancing age, AF, anemia, pulmonary embolism, critical illness and burns; NICE 1.2.7 (followed here) does not list age or AF

decision_facts.group: Things that push NT-proBNP down: obesity, already on a diuretic / ACE inhibitor / ARNI / ARB / beta blocker / MRA
decision_facts.why: A 'normal' value can be falsely reassuring in these patients. NICE (1.2.7) also notes levels run lower on average in people of African or African-Caribbean background, so a low value is less reassuring; the cause is not established. Context for the specialist only - Lantern never uses race as an input.

decision_facts.group: Prior heart attack, coronary disease, valve disease, high BP, AFib
decision_facts.why: The common causes of heart failure

decision_facts.group: Other causes of swelling: kidney disease, amlodipine, liver disease, low albumin
decision_facts.why: Ankle swelling may not be the heart at all
decision_facts.source_note: Only the amlodipine part is sourced (2025 BP Table 13: dihydropyridine CCBs cause dose-related lower-extremity edema). Kidney disease, liver disease and low albumin are draft.

decision_facts.group: Medicines that can worsen heart failure: NSAIDs, pioglitazone, diltiazem, verapamil
decision_facts.why: Stopping them may help while waiting - specialist decides
decision_facts.source_note: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF 7.3.7: NSAIDs worsen HF and should be avoided or withdrawn (3: Harm, B-NR); thiazolidinediones e.g. pioglitazone (3: Harm, A); diltiazem/verapamil (3: Harm, A) - all stated for HFrEF; 6.1 rec 7: thiazolidinediones should not be used with LVEF <50%. Also NICE NG106 1.4.12 (diltiazem/verapamil).

decision_facts.why: Anemia, iron deficiency and thyroid disease cause or worsen breathlessness
decision_facts.source_note: Also 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF 4.1.1 rec 2 (CBC, iron studies, TSH in initial labs) and 10.1: iron deficiency = ferritin <100, or 100-300 with transferrin saturation <20%; IV iron reasonable in HFrEF with iron deficiency (2a, B-R)

decision_facts.group: Current status: weight, BP, potassium, diuretic, known heart failure
decision_facts.why: Baseline for daily weights and for any diuretic change

tests_first.source_note: Also 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF 4.1.1 rec 2 (COR 1, C-EO): initial labs include CBC, urinalysis, electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Mg), BUN, creatinine, glucose, lipids, liver tests, iron studies, TSH

routing_rules.note: eGFR under 30 - heart failure team should liaise with a kidney specialist
NT-proBNP under 400 without heart failure medicines - heart failure less likely; NICE suggests discussing with a heart failure specialist if still concerned
On amlodipine with no other sign of heart failure - ankle swelling may be the medicine (PCP medicine change)
routing_rules.source_note: Amlodipine edema: 2025 BP Table 13. Routing to eConsult is a draft judgment.

not_seen: Ankle swelling from a medicine such as amlodipine (PCP med change may be enough)
review_notes: Is 2 weeks = 'urgent' the right mapping for a US clinic? (NICE 2-week rule is UK)
2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline (US, full text checked) gives no outpatient referral time-frames, so NICE NG106 timings stay; US 8.1 rec 1: timely referral to HF specialty care for ADVANCED HF (COR 1)

Red flags (breathless at rest, chest pain, fainting) come from the CLAUDE.md table, not NG106; the 2022 US HF guideline (full text checked) also has no outpatient red-flag list - its shock criteria (9.5, Table 22) and advanced-HF indicators (8.1, Table 18) are hospital/advanced-stage

Salt substitutes: NICE HF 1.9.11 says avoid potassium-based salt substitutes; the 2025 US BP guideline (5.1, COR 2a) says they can help lower BP except with CKD or potassium-retaining drugs. Kept NICE wording for heart failure - clinician to confirm

abnormal_ecg.label: Abnormal ECG

red_flags.text: Signs of an ongoing heart attack
Complete or high-grade heart block with symptoms (fainting, dizziness, breathlessness)
red_flags.source_note: Tier not sourced; 'bifascicular', 'trifascicular' and '2:1 block' in the pattern are questionable for this flag.

red_flags.text: Very slow heart rate with fainting, near-fainting, confusion, low blood pressure, chest pain or breathlessness at rest
red_flags.source_note: Symptom list follows the ACLS adult bradycardia algorithm (signs of poor perfusion), cited from memory - not checked. No numeric 'very slow' rate in the checked guideline material; the cutoff <40 bpm is a draft number for clinician review.

urgent_flags.text: Heart rate below 40 while awake, or a slow rate (awake or asleep) with dizziness or tiredness (check rate-slowing medicines, thyroid, potassium)
urgent_flags.source_note: Draft tier for clinician review. 2018 bradycardia guideline (ACC news summary): slow rates without symptoms usually need no treatment and nocturnal slowing alone is not a pacing indication - fit people and sleep can run below 40.

urgent_flags.text: Mobitz II, 2:1, high-grade or complete heart block - even without symptoms (pacemaker usually indicated)
urgent_flags.source_note: Supported: pacing recommended for acquired Mobitz II, high-grade or third-degree AV block not due to a reversible cause, regardless of symptoms. 'Urgent' tier is Lantern's judgment.

urgent_flags.text: Long QT (QTc 500 or more is high risk)
urgent_flags.source_note: Partly supported (search excerpt only): QTc over 500 ms flags torsade risk, but the 2010 statement is about hospitalized patients.

card_hints.text: Slow heart rate reported during sleep - often normal on its own; consider screening for sleep apnea
card_hints.source_note: Summary: nocturnal bradycardia alone is not a pacing indication and is an opportunity to screen for sleep apnea. Shown on the card only; never changes the tier.

decision_facts.why: The first question is whether the finding is new or old

decision_facts.group: Prior heart attack or coronary disease
decision_facts.why: Old heart attacks leave lasting ECG changes

decision_facts.group: Medicines that slow the heart or conduction: beta blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone
decision_facts.why: A reversible cause of slow rhythms and blocks
decision_facts.source_note: Partly supported (ACC summary only): pacing applies when the cause is not reversible; a medicine review is implied, the specific list is not given.

decision_facts.group: QT-prolonging medicines (e.g. citalopram, ondansetron, azithromycin, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol, methadone, sotalol, amiodarone)
decision_facts.why: Common, fixable cause of long QT
decision_facts.source_note: Partly supported (search excerpt only): inpatient statement.

decision_facts.why: Low potassium/magnesium/calcium prolong QT; thyroid and potassium affect slow rhythms
decision_facts.source_note: Partly supported (search excerpt only): low potassium and magnesium are torsade risk factors; calcium and thyroid not confirmed.

decision_facts.why: Can cause slow heart rates and pauses at night
A slow rate points to a conduction problem or a medicine effect

low_concern_findings: Isolated right bundle branch block without symptoms

routing_rules.note: Prior heart attack or coronary disease - Q waves or ST/T changes may be old; compare with a prior ECG

not_seen: Unchanged old findings in a patient with no symptoms - often an eConsult answer
Low-concern findings listed in low_concern_findings - usually eConsult
review_notes: Long QT is not covered by the 2018 bradycardia guideline - source and 500 ms cutoff need confirming
How to treat a bundle branch block when no prior ECG exists to show it is new
Echo recommendation for new LBBB - verify in 2018 guideline

hard_to_control_bp_chol.label: Hard-to-control blood pressure or cholesterol

red_flags.text: BP over 180/120 with signs of organ damage: chest pain, confusion, vision change, severe headache, weakness, breathlessness (hypertensive emergency - ER)

urgent_flags.text: BP over 180/120 without signs of organ damage (severe hypertension - not an ER visit; outpatient medicine adjustment)
urgent_flags.source_note: Severe hypertension is defined in 2025 BP guideline 6.2 / Fig 9, which says treat in the outpatient setting with close follow-up within 4 weeks and no ED referral. The guideline gives no specialist-referral urgency, so the 'urgent' tier here is not guideline-backed (it came from the CLAUDE.md table and the old term 'hypertensive urgency').

card_hints.text: High BP with low potassium - screen for primary aldosteronism (aldosterone/renin ratio)
card_hints.source_note: Guideline: hypokalemia (spontaneous or diuretic-induced) is a reason to screen, not an urgency criterion. 3.5 mmol/L is the usual lower limit of normal; the guideline gives no number.

decision_facts.group: Recent BP readings (trend, not one value)
decision_facts.why: Confirms BP is truly uncontrolled. Guideline goal is under 130/80 for all adults; judge on an average of readings from 2+ visits, not one value

decision_facts.group: Number and classes of BP medicines, including whether one is a diuretic
decision_facts.why: Resistant hypertension = above goal on 3 medicines (one a diuretic) at good doses, or needing 4+

decision_facts.group: Things that raise BP: NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, steroids, some antidepressants and antipsychotics, oral contraceptives, transplant drugs, heavy alcohol
decision_facts.why: A common, fixable cause of 'resistant' BP

decision_facts.group: Clues to a secondary cause: low potassium, sleep apnea, kidney disease, young age
decision_facts.why: 2025 guideline: screen for primary aldosteronism with resistant hypertension (whatever the potassium), low potassium, sleep apnea, an adrenal mass, or a family history of early hypertension or stroke under 40

decision_facts.group: Signs of damage from BP: kidney function, urine albumin, prior stroke or heart disease
decision_facts.why: Raises urgency and the strength of treatment

decision_facts.group: LDL trend, statin dose, and any statin intolerance
decision_facts.why: LDL 190+ suggests inherited high cholesterol; on-statin LDL above goal may need added therapy

decision_facts.group: Existing heart disease, stroke or diabetes
decision_facts.why: Sets how low LDL and BP should go

tests_first.source_note: Basic test for hypertension (3.1.2); condition keeps it off cholesterol-only referrals - draft

3.2.3.1 rec 1: screen in resistant hypertension (COR 1, regardless of potassium), hypokalemia, sleep apnea, adrenal incidentaloma, family history of early-onset hypertension or stroke <40. '3+ BP medicines' is a proxy for resistant; incidentaloma and family history are not in the fact list yet. Still not pre-checked.

routing_rules.note: Resistant pattern or low potassium - specialist look for a secondary cause
Regular NSAID use can raise BP - a medicine review may be enough before a visit
routing_rules.source_note: NSAIDs raising BP: 2025 BP Table 13 interfering medicines (verify row). eConsult routing is a draft judgment.

not_seen: Often answerable by eConsult (medicine adjustment advice) without a visit
Suspected primary aldosteronism or other hormone cause (endocrinology)
review_notes: Whether bp_severe_no_symptoms belongs in 'urgent': 2025 guideline says the PCP intensifies medicines now with follow-up within 4 weeks (Fig 9)
The 2025 BP guideline does not cover BP management in coronary disease, heart failure, AFib, valve, aortic disease or PAD (1.4)
Cholesterol source (2018 AHA/ACC) not yet checked
Severe hypertension without organ damage kept URGENT (option A) until NICE NG136 1.5.x is checked; the 2025 US guideline (6.2, Fig 9) would place it in 'soon' (follow-up within 4 weeks)

review_questions: Are these the right red flags, and is anything emergent missing?
Should a stress test / coronary CT be pre-checked for chest pain, or always left to cardiology?
Is new AFib with a fast rate urgent, or emergent above some rate?

Heart-rate cutoffs are drafts: fast AFib = rate above 110 at rest; very slow = below 40. Slow + fainting/near-fainting/confusion/low BP/chest pain/breathless at rest = emergent; below 40 alone, or slow + dizziness/tiredness = urgent. Are these right, should athlete readings be excluded? (Sleep-only readings no longer count without symptoms; they get a card note instead.)
Do NICE's 2-week / 6-week heart failure rules map well onto urgent / routine in a US clinic?
BP: should the chart's own BP readings (last 14 days) count, or only what the PCP wrote?
For abnormal ECG, how should Lantern treat a bundle branch block when no prior ECG shows it is new?
Which reasons are most often fully answerable by eConsult?
Is a 'soon' tier (about 4-6 weeks) between urgent and routine useful in a US clinic, and which flags belong in it?
